findings.location: Section 1.B "The absence, and who holds the missing data" — the sentence "Investor filings were checked; Spotify's tier retention above is the only hit."
findings.issue: The draft asserts an investor-filing audit that the depth investigation explicitly records as NOT performed, and states no search record at all for the absence claim that the whole section rests on. Per this run's inference-depth directive, an audited absence must state what was searched; here the draft states something that was searched and wasn't.
findings.evidence: interim-report-attrition-telemetry-absence, "What the new sources say": "I did not complete the third sub-task (searching platform investor filings — Bilibili 20-F, Kuaishou IPO prospectus, Spotify 20-F/Loud & Clear, Roblox S-1, Patreon's public reports) within budget; the fetcher spent the bulk of its calls chasing the Wikipedia citation chain... I cannot state that no platform has ever disclosed such a figure, only that I did not find one and did not exhaustively search for one." Same note, Confidence field: "medium-high on the 'no telemetry exists' claim — five independent search angles (three prior OpenAlex sweeps, plus my own academic-API searches and TubeCensus's own literature review) all came back empty, but I did not exhaust the investor-filing/S-1 angle." The note's own academic-API angles are named as Wikipedia, OSS, Bilibili/Douyin, AfreecaTV/SOOP.
findings.recommendation: Replace the unsupported 'Investor filings were checked' clause with the actual, defensible search record at roughly equal length: three OpenAlex sweeps in step 2, academic-API searches across four language/platform angles (Chinese Bilibili/Douyin, Korean AfreecaTV/SOOP, plus the Wikipedia and open-source analogue literatures), and TubeCensus's own literature review — all returning zero platform-scale creator-survival studies. Keep the Spotify row but present it as a hit found rather than as the yield of a completed filings audit, and state that the S-1/20-F angle was not exhausted, so the absence is well-audited on the academic side and unexhausted on the disclosure side. If a later pipeline step actually did run the filings search, name what was checked instead.

findings.location: Section 2.B, the living-wage matrix table and the paragraph beginning "Regner reports the same roughly 250 creators..." — specifically "raises the 0.043% share by roughly an order of magnitude"
findings.issue: The threshold lever is the second of the two decomposition components the draft leans on, and the draft states it only as 'roughly an order of magnitude' when the interim note computes the exact recut from Rieder's own published table. This is the highest-value single number missing from the report: it is the same-dataset, same-denominator counterpart to the 5.75x denominator swing the draft does print, and the matrix table has an empty slot for it.
findings.evidence: interim-report-living-wage-share-magnitude, Rieder paragraph: "Their Table 1 gives channel counts and average annual ad revenue per subscriber tier: Diamond (10M+ subs) 517 channels, avg $1,707,446/yr; Gold (1M-10M) 14,969, avg $165,892; Silver (100k-1M) 138,284, avg $16,346; Bronze (10k-100k) 769,472, avg $2,058; Opal (1k-10k) 3,491,938, avg $295; <1k subscribers 31,727,531 channels, 0% of revenue. Total channels: 36,142,711... at the US federal minimum-wage-equivalent annual floor (~$15,080), Silver-tier-and-above clears it — (517+14,969+138,284)/36,142,711 = 0.43%. At the 2020 US median household income (~$67,521), only Diamond+Gold clear it — (517+14,969)/36,142,711 = 0.043% — Same dataset, same denominator, 10x difference purely from threshold choice."
findings.recommendation: Add a 0.43% row to the section 2.B matrix directly under the existing 0.043% row: threshold '~$15,080/yr (US federal minimum-wage equivalent)', denominator 'All crawled channels', same n (~36.1m), same year/platform/country, type 'Arithmetic re-cut of the authors' published tier table, not a figure they state'. Then replace 'by roughly an order of magnitude' in the prose with the exact pair (0.043% to 0.43%, i.e. exactly 10x) and cite the two tier counts that produce it (517 + 14,969 = the median-household numerator; + 138,284 Silver = the minimum-wage numerator). Roughly length-neutral, since the vague clause is dropped.

findings.issue: The draft carries the Graphtreon row but strips out both its numerators and its analytical payload. The interim note treats this row as a second, independent measurement of the threshold lever (2.2x on an identical population) AND as an independent cross-dataset convergence with Regner at a comparable bar — two findings, neither of which survives into the report. The draft also cites only the Outline write-up, not the source note that carries the counts.
findings.evidence: interim-report-living-wage-share-magnitude: "Digital Music News (`less-than-2-of-content-creators-on-patreon-earn-monthly-minimum-wage`), Oct 2017, n=79,420 tracked Patreon creators... 'only 1,393 creators (under 2%) earned the federal monthly minimum wage of $1,160 a month' — 1.75%. 'If changed to $15 per hour, only 0.8%, or 635 creators, made that amount' — a 2.2x swing from threshold choice alone, on the identical population... at a comparable ~$2,500-2,600/month bar the two studies — two years apart, different methodology — converge on roughly 1%: Regner 1.03%, Graphtreon 0.8%."
findings.recommendation: Put the two numerators into the matrix row (1,393 of 79,420 at $1,160/mo; 635 at a $15/hour equivalent) and add one clause to the decomposition paragraph noting that Graphtreon reproduces the threshold lever independently at 2.2x on an identical population, and that Regner's 1.03% (2013-15, transaction record) and Graphtreon's 0.8% (Oct 2017, public-page aggregation) converge on roughly one percent at a comparable ~$2,500/month bar despite different years and methods. Add the [[less-than-2-of-content-creators-on-patreon-earn-monthly-minimum-wage]] citation alongside the Outline one.

findings.location: Section 2.B, final sentence of the paragraph beginning "Regner reports the same roughly 250 creators" — "Those two levers, on identical data, account for much of the apparent hundredfold telemetry-versus-survey gap without any appeal to measurement error."
findings.issue: This is a derived claim that does not name the arithmetic it derives from. 'Much of' is doing work that the interim note does with multiplication. Per the inference-depth directive, a derived claim must name its sourced inputs; here the two inputs are already in the paragraph and their product is never stated, so the reader cannot check the inference.
findings.evidence: interim-report-living-wage-share-magnitude, section (4) The residual: "Multiplying even conservative estimates of the three levers — denominator (~5-6x, per Regner), threshold (~10x within-country per Rieder), and sampling bias... yields a combined multiplier in the 250x-600x range, which is the same order of magnitude as the observed headline gap." Constrained by the evidence digest's own correction (temp/evidence-digest.md, living-wage contested cluster): "It demonstrates that popularity-gated sampling inflates prevalence estimates roughly tenfold on a DIFFERENT quantity... it is NOT a measured coefficient for income and must never be presented as one."
findings.recommendation: State the product of the two measured levers explicitly — 5.75x denominator times 10x threshold is roughly 58x, against an observed survey-versus-telemetry gap running from 0.043% to 63% — and then say plainly that the third component (sampling frame) is known in direction but has never been measured for income, so no total is computable. Do NOT import the interim note's 250-600x figure; the digest's correction forbids treating the 36.7%/3.49% pair as an income coefficient, and section 6.A already handles that correctly. This swaps a vague quantifier for named arithmetic at roughly equal length.

findings.location: Section 2.A table, UK IPO row ("£20,160 men / £13,057 women; £51,816 major-label / £12,944 self-releasing | 37% ≤£5,000; 62% ≤£20,000; 9% >£50,000"), and section 2.D
findings.issue: The draft omits the single most analytically load-bearing cut in the UK IPO instrument: the n=197 subgroup for whom music was the sole income. The interim note flags this as the survey-side evidence that independently corroborates the telemetry-side conclusion — a self-selected instrument that still fails to show a living-wage majority once its own most-relevant filter is applied. Without it the draft leaves the survey/telemetry split looking cleaner than the evidence is.
findings.evidence: interim-report-living-wage-share-magnitude: "of the 197 respondents for whom music was their sole income, 43% earned ≤£20,000/year, against a national-minimum-wage-equivalent full-time salary of £17,076 — i.e., a large fraction of even self-selected survey respondents who say music is their only income sit at or near minimum wage. Notably, this self-selected sample also fails to show a living-wage majority — it is not just telemetry that finds low rates; the corpus's own most-detailed Western survey does too, once the 'only source of income' filter is applied honestly." Corroborated in temp/evidence-digest.md: "n=197 | 43% <= GBP 20,000 | 64% <= GBP 30,000 | minimum wage GBP 8.21/hour | GBP 17,076 annualised at 2,080 hours".
findings.recommendation: Add the sole-income cut to the UK IPO row or to the section 2.D paragraph: among the 197 respondents whose only income was music, 43% earned £20,000 or less and 64% £30,000 or less, against a 2019 minimum-wage-equivalent full-time salary of £17,076. One clause, and it turns a Side-A instrument into corroboration of the Side-B conclusion the report reaches.

findings.location: Section 4.B "What models of actual continuation find" — the sentence beginning "Törhönen's structural model of 377 creators finds intrinsic motivation predicting intention to continue at p=0.000..."
findings.issue: The draft cites the Törhönen SEM but drops the companion ANOVA entirely, which the interim note calls 'a decisive falsification test for the crude money-keeps-people-in story'. That test is the only place in the corpus where income orientation and actual tenure are put in the same table, and it is exactly the claim section 4.B is making — so the section argues its thesis from intention data while the direct tenure test sits unused.
findings.evidence: interim-report-quit-driver-money-vs-motivation: "The HICSS-52 companion study (ANOVA, n=382, same 2017 fieldwork) adds a decisive falsification test for the crude 'money keeps people in' story: creators who self-identify their content creation as 'work' earn the most (mean $774.85/month) and put in the most hours (25/week) — but their tenure (34.21 months) is statistically indistinguishable from the 'play'-oriented group (38.67 months) and the 'playbour' group (33.95 months) in every pairwise Tukey comparison (p=0.999, 0.657, 0.544). Income-orientation predicts earnings and hours; it does not predict how long anyone stays."
findings.recommendation: Add one sentence to section 4.B carrying the three group tenures and the Tukey non-significance: work-oriented creators earn the most ($774.85/month mean) and work the most (25 h/week) but their 34.21-month tenure is statistically indistinguishable from the play group's 38.67 and the playbour group's 33.95 (n=382, 2017, all pairwise Tukey p≥0.544). Cite [[play-playbour-or-labour-the-relationships-between-perception-of]], already in the draft's citation set.

findings.location: Section 4.B — "Superchat income shows no significant main effect (β=−0.136, p=0.111)" and the framing sentence "Four designs model persistence rather than feeling, and none finds income level operative."
findings.issue: The draft reports only the main effect and therefore overstates the null. Zhao's model does find a significant income-by-time interaction; the honest reading is that income's protective effect is small and accumulates gradually, not that income is inert. The draft also compresses the affiliation result: it reports the 1.980 small-agency hazard without the fact that independent VTubers are statistically indistinguishable from large-agency ones, which is what makes the finding structural-access rather than resource-level.
findings.evidence: interim-report-quit-driver-money-vs-motivation: "Total Superchat Income's main effect on hazard is not statistically significant (β=−0.136, p=0.111) — but its interaction with time is (p=0.010), meaning income's protective effect is small and only accumulates gradually... The single strongest, most significant predictor is affiliation status: non-large-agency VTubers face 1.98x the hazard of large-agency VTubers (p=0.003), while independent VTubers are statistically indistinguishable from large-agency VTubers in this model (p=0.302)."
findings.recommendation: Append the interaction to the existing parenthetical — income's main effect is not significant (β=−0.136, p=0.111) but its interaction with time is (p=0.010), so the protective effect is small and cumulative rather than absent — and soften 'none finds income level operative' to a claim about income as a continuous level-predictor. Add the p=0.302 for independents-versus-large-agency, which is what identifies the operative variable as structural access rather than agency resources per se.

findings.location: Section 3, the paragraph beginning "Three independent measurements find output volume and threshold-crossing, not elapsed tenure, to be operative." — specifically its third leg, "Among Patreon's 24,257 funded campaigns about 20% received exactly one pledge."
findings.issue: The claim of three independent measurements is derived, and one of the three named claims does not support it: the Patreon one-pledge concentration fact says nothing about tenure versus output. The interim note's triangulation is Rieder / Bärtl / Wollborn, and the draft has silently substituted a non-supporting third source for the real one — while also dropping Bärtl's qualification, which is the only thing on the record that partially cuts against the reframe.
findings.evidence: interim-report-time-to-income-reframe-tenure-vs-output, Evidence weight: "3 large-sample/telemetry measurements support the reframe (Rieder n=36.3M channels; vidIQ n=1,027,773 channels; Wollborn n=18,467 streamers)", and on Bärtl: "The abstract itself is still informative and partially qualifies the tenure-doesn't-matter reading: 'older channels have a significantly higher probability to garner a large viewership, but... there has always been a small chance for young channels to become successful quickly, depending on whether they choose their genre wisely.' No correlation coefficients or sample size are recoverable from the abstract... This is an audited absence: the peer-reviewed anchor for 'does age predict success' exists... and is functionally unreadable behind a publisher paywall with no legal open mirror (SAGE eprint, ResearchGate mirror, and Hochschule Offenburg OPUS all Cloudflare-blocked or abstract-only)."
findings.recommendation: Replace the Patreon one-pledge clause with the Bärtl leg, carrying its qualification and its access status at equal length: the paper Rieder replicates finds older channels significantly more likely to reach large viewership but with a persistent small chance of fast young-channel success conditional on genre, and its coefficients are unrecoverable — SAGE, ResearchGate and the Offenburg institutional repository are all blocked or abstract-only — so Rieder's 0.082/0.101/0.009/0.003 are the only quantified version of this relationship on the record. Cite [[opus-4-youtube-channels-uploads-and-views-a-statistical-analysis-of-the-past-10]].

findings.location: Section 5.C, the paragraph beginning "The chart is page 10 of TikTok's commissioned report..." and/or section 6.C's closing paragraph on the Indonesian figure
findings.issue: The report builds the denominator lever in section 2.B and then declines to apply it to the one Southeast Asian number it has, leaving the 63% and the Western telemetry figures looking two to three orders of magnitude apart when the interim note shows they close to within one order once the same denominator convention is used. This is the report's own analytical device, developed at length in section 2, going unused exactly where the query's SEA question needs it.
findings.evidence: interim-report-living-wage-share-magnitude: "Recomputed on TikTok's own full-MAU denominator rather than its self-selected 'already monetized' denominator: 8M/125M = 6.4% of all Indonesian TikTok users monetize at all; 63% of that 6.4% clears UMR = ≈4.0% of all Indonesian TikTok MAU. That recalculated 4% figure is within roughly one order of magnitude of the Western telemetry figures (0.04–1.6%) — not two to three — once the SAME 'all accounts' denominator convention is applied." The 125 million MAU figure is on the DPR record per interim-report-sea-evidence-provenance-and-breadth: "125 million MAU, 8 million creators of whom 63% earn above minimum wage."
findings.recommendation: Add one sentence applying the section 2.B denominator lever to the Indonesian figures: against TikTok's own stated 125 million Indonesian monthly active users, 8 million monetizing creators is 6.4%, and 63% of that is roughly 4% of all Indonesian TikTok accounts — within one order of magnitude of the Western full-population telemetry figures rather than two or three. Label it explicitly as an arithmetic recut of two figures from the same platform self-disclosure, not a measurement, and keep the existing provenance caveats intact.

findings.location: Section 5.D table, rows "Thailand", "Philippines", and "Vietnam, Singapore, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Brunei, Timor-Leste — Documented absence"
findings.issue: Three 'documented absence' verdicts are asserted with no statement of what was searched, which the run's inference-depth directive specifically prohibits. The interim note holds a detailed per-country search record — including national-statistics-office queries and local-language query strings — and one country's row is wrong in kind: Singapore is filed under 'no measurement' when the note recovered a specific if unverified figure.
findings.evidence: interim-report-sea-evidence-provenance-and-breadth: "Searches in Thai ('รายได้ยูทูปเบอร์', 'อาชีพครีเอเตอร์ สถิติ', 'อินฟลูเอนเซอร์ รายได้ สำรวจ') plus a targeted NSO Thailand query returned only top-earner puff pieces...; NSO Thailand's Labour Force Survey (2023 wave, 76,735 households) shows no evidence of coding content creator as a distinct occupation." "Malaysia's DOSM tracks gig/informal workers (559k-4M depending on definition; median informal-worker income RM2,000 vs. national median RM3,600) with no content-creator breakout." "Singapore produced one promising but unconfirmed lead: trade press cites an IMDA 2024 survey finding roughly 8% of Singaporeans aged 18-35 identify content creation as a primary income source or career goal, typical income S$2,500-6,000/month, with no CPF, paid leave, or health insurance... Both article fetches hit hard paywalls... This claim survives only as a low-confidence, unverified search-snippet-level assertion."
findings.recommendation: Convert the bare 'Documented absence' verdicts into audited absences by naming the instruments queried, at roughly equal length: Thailand — Thai-language search plus the NSO Labour Force Survey (2023 wave, 76,735 households), which codes no content-creator occupation; Malaysia — DOSM's gig/informal series (559k–4m depending on definition; median informal income RM2,000 against a national RM3,600) with no creator breakout; Vietnam — Vietnamese-language search returning only Western-data pass-throughs. Split Singapore out of the blanket-absence row into its own row as an unverified lead: an IMDA 2024 survey reported in paywalled trade press at roughly 8% of 18-35-year-olds treating creation as a primary income source or career goal, S$2,500–6,000/month, original publication not located — flagged as a research gap, not a citable finding.

findings.location: Section 1.B, the sentence "One vendor source claiming to be this telemetry is excluded: its posts give three sample sizes for one 2019 cohort — 97,601, 105,891, and over 50,000 — with no named analyst or methodology..."
findings.issue: The draft's disqualification is less precise than the interim note's, and precision matters here because this exclusion is what licenses the report's 'no telemetry exists' finding. Two of the three numbers do reconcile arithmetically; only one pair is a genuine contradiction, and that pair sits inside a single post — its title against its own body. Stating it the draft's way invites a rebuttal that the note has already pre-empted.
findings.evidence: interim-report-attrition-telemetry-absence: "A single post's own title says '97,601 Creators' while its own body says '105,891... channels.'... the growth-factors post explicitly claims its 50K+ sample is drawn from... the same dataset... Breakout 13,464 + Growing 7,028 + Stalling 3,425 + Fading 24,766 = 48,683 — which is at least arithmetically close to 'over 50,000,' so this one relation is plausible; but the 97,601-vs-105,891 discrepancy for what the half-life post calls the identical tracked cohort has no such reconciling arithmetic." Committed position: "an internal numerical contradiction (97,601 vs. 105,891 channels for what it presents as one tracked cohort) that alone disqualifies it."
findings.recommendation: Narrow the charge to the dispositive one at equal length: the half-life post's own title says 97,601 channels while its body says 105,891 for what it presents as one tracked cohort, with no reconciling arithmetic — while the third post's 'over 50,000' does plausibly reconcile as the sum of the survival post's four non-dormant buckets (48,683). Keep the absent-authorship and left-truncation points as they stand.

findings.location: Section 3, the sentence "A channel at the eligibility line earning the modal few dollars a month would need on the order of a year and a half of accrual to cross the $100 threshold"
findings.issue: A vague duration where the interim note has a sourced range derived from named telemetry. The draft's own gate table already carries the vidIQ row that produces the range, so the vagueness costs the reader the one arithmetic bridge between the eligibility gate and the payout gate that the depth investigation calls the most load-bearing in the locus.
findings.evidence: interim-report-time-to-income-reframe-tenure-vs-output: "vidIQ's telemetry (n=1,027,773 channels at 1,000-1,100 subscribers, measured May 2026) puts the median channel at this eligibility band earning under $5-20/month — meaning a channel exactly at the eligibility line would need roughly 5-20+ months of accrual just to cross the $100 payout floor, quite apart from review-queue delay. This is the single most load-bearing bridge in the whole locus: eligibility and payout are temporally decoupled by an order of magnitude for the modal channel."
findings.recommendation: Replace 'on the order of a year and a half' with the sourced range — roughly five to twenty-plus months, depending where in the under-$5-to-$20/month band the channel sits (vidIQ, n=1,027,773 channels at 1,000-1,100 subscribers, May 2026) — and keep the existing 'before review-queue delay' qualifier. Length-neutral.
